institutionName: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was especially motivated by the prospect of visitng a part of the United States, where I don't think I would have gone otherwise. It also appealed to me that UNC Chapel Hill is such an old and charming campus, heightening the feel of an "authentic" college experience.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Only drawback being the administrative and logstical part of it - some of it having to do with the school's protocol, but mostly just unforeseen matters that took up just a little more energy than I wash they had.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Since you already have your UNC e-mail set up before leaving for your stay, you can feel pretty confident that you will receive all necessary information there, or at least have someone to ask. Nicole, who is in charge of the exchange programme is the absolute best, and went above and beyond to make sure we felt prepared for our exchange.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As mentioned before, Nicole offered a lot of assistance. We were also made aware of a What'sApp group that we could join beforehand, where current exchange students were also available for answering questions that we might have.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it relatively easy to find housing off campus. On the UNC website, under "Housing", they have gathered som links to external sites for finding accommodation. They are not affiliated with the school, but come recommended. I used the site "Roomadillo" which I found super accessible and easy to navigate in. Most of the accommodation there were subleases for a semester only, which is what you need as an exchange student - from what I've heard it can be challenging if you don't find a sublease, beacause the minimum lenght for rental contracts is usually a year. So obviously, a lot of the people renting out their rooms were also going on exchange, which was why they had a vacancy for a semester, and that also made for a perfect conversation starter when reaching out to them. Most of the listings will have a direct link to an e-mail or Facebook profile, from where it is super easy to contact people. I think I was in touch with one or two people, before I found a good match. I ended up living at Lark, which is an apartment complex approximately 10-15 minutes walking distance from the main street, Franklin Street, and more or less the same distance from campus (depending on which part of campus you are going to)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I believe off campus housing is overall more expensive than on-campus, but in my experience it was absolutely worth it. As mentioned before, I subleased a room in an apartment at Lark, where all rooms have a connected bathroom, so it's almost like having your own little apartment within the apartment. You then have a shared open kitchen and living room, as well as a balcony/terrace. I really liked the fact that I could cook my own meals, and also that I could shut a door and be by myself when needed. When you live on campus, you will most likely share a dorm room with a roommate, it's quite close quarters, and you're almost certainly forced to get the meal plan, which is obviously fine if you don't mind eating all your meals in the dining hall (which can also be a fun experience from time to time, but if you're like me, you like having the option to choose for yourself). I enjoyed the 10-15 minute walk to campus/the main street, but there were also shuttles running almost all day, and I am pretty sure that goes for most apartment complexes off campus aimed at UNC students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you want the "true" college experince, on campus housing can be fine, but if you like your personal space, like preparing your own food and genereally just having more space and something more like a proper home, it is definitely worth spending som more money on off campus housing.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It should be noted, that course registration is very different from KU. There are so many more courses to choose from, and it is very important to research which courses are offered in which semesters, as some courses may only be offered in the spring term, others only the fall term.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You register on the school's general portal, ConnectCarolina, which is also where you'll pay for on campus housing, meal plans, and any other fees that go directly to the school. It's also where your transcript will be uploaded, where you can see your class schedules once you are registered, and more or less everything that has to do with your semester at UNC. As exchange students, we are in the last "wave" of enrollment, which means that the American students have first pick of all the classes offered. The first thing you are advised to do, is look through the course cataloque, and add courses to your "shopping cart" this can be done before your enrollment slot opens up, and I would definitely recommend doing this at the first chance you get. You will then receive a designated slot for enrollment, which is time specific, and it is likewise recommended that you are ready at that time, because courses get filled up quickly. What is very, very important to remember is, that this process is super chaotic, and everyone (teachers included) are very well aware of that. For the sake of the exchange you are required to be enrolled in the number of credits that have been specified, but just know, that most likely, these are not the courses you will end up taking. The first week of classes is "shopping week", where class registration is still open, and you can switch around according to availability. You will be urged to contact the proffessors of courses that are full, but that you might need as a specific requirement from your home institution, or that you just have a certain interest in, and in most cases, it will be possible to work around logistics. My best advice is just to trust the process and know, that one way or another, you will end up with the right amount of credits, and courses that fit your needs.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There were several guides available through the exchange portal and UNCs website in general, but it was hard figuring out, which courses were offered when. I also experienced some classes having one description in the registration portal, but then being introduced to have completely different contents when I showed up for the first day of classes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I found out, that a lot of the film related classes that had first caught my attention in the course catalogue, weren't offered in the spring semester, where I had my exchange. Make sure to check up on this as soon as you are able to - I am pretty sure it can be done through ConnectCarolina. As there weren't any specific requirements for the courses I had to take, I had a little fun with registering for a course such as "Chinese Science Fiction", which I ended up really enjoying! Of course, you have to have your courses approved from KU. Apart from the fact that many of the courses I had had my eye on weren't offered in the term I was there for, I found it relatively easy to register for the classes I wanted. Obiously, some classes will just be so popular, or restricted in some way, that it is almost impossible, and I had a couple of those experiences, but ended up just accepting that I wouldn't get in to those.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Start researching courses as soon as you are able to. Also, do yourself a favour and check out the proffessors of the courses on
ratemyprofessor.com
. Don't hesitate to get a little pushy if professors don't reply to your e-mails, and honestly just trust the process, bacuse 99.9% of the time, things will work out in the end. Once again, Nicole is also a great asset during this process - ask her!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were not necessarily more difficult than at KU, but they were definitely structured differently, and have higher expectations regarding participation. The courses all have numbers, and they state the level, so the higher the number, the higher the level - the degree to which this acutally held true was differing.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As mentioned before, the expectations regarding participation are quite different. For each course, the teacher will share how they make up your final grade, and oftentimes class participation and attendance make up a certain percentage of your final grade. Then, most of the classes I had also had small, weekly assignments that all counted towards the final grade. In my experience, it did feel like the expectations were higher, as well as the overall workload, but it also meant that everything didn't just depend on your final exam. Additionally, the written exams at the end of the semester were often less lenghty and comprehensive than what we are used to at KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
History of American Sreenwriting (COMM 430)
Chinese Science Fiction (CMPL 545)
Literature and Cinema (ENGL 381)
Introduction to Gender Communication (WGST 224)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend History of American screenwriting to scholars of film and media - or others interested in the course. It is a little like Film History, but the angle is a little different, as are the movies highlighted. I also really enjoyed Chinese Science Fiction, just because it was so completely different than the courses I usually take.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It's hard to say specifically, but I was generally surprised at the cost of living - most of the time it's at least as expensive as Copenhagen, if not more. Buses are free, which is quite great, but many times we would end up Ubering, which is obviously an extra expense

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books are pretty expensive. It is almost always possible to rent books, and this is really great option, since you probably won't be bringing them back with you anyways. Generally I would say, the estimated costs that the school present, at set very low. I spent quite a bit more than I though I would, but it all depends on how much you spend on trips, going out, groceries etc.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were many different clubs to attend, and as exchange students we were automatically able to take advantage of the recreation centers, and could also sign up for all the different sports and workout classes that were offered. I did a variety of yoga, pilates and barre classes, and they were really relly great. The instructors are mostly students, but very very capable and it was just an amazing thing to be able to do, without having to pay for a gym membership. The pool is also open outside of the swim club's training hours, and I highly recommend taking advantage of that as well.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There were som many different activities available and I would recommend attending as many of them as possible! Sports is a huge thing at UNC - fall is football season, and spring is basketball season. I would definitely recommend going to some of the games!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Definitely walk out to Carrboro on the weekends or whenever you have the time - it's a little bigger than Chapel Hill, there's a farmer's market on the weekends and the vibe is just A+. 
If you get the chance, visit Asheville - it's a bit of a drive, but it's really beautiful, and the town itself is great. 
I took a hiking trip out to Stone Mountain, which was organized by the school activity center, but I know that North Carolina is generally known for having really great hiking spots, so I would definitely check that out too! 
Wilmington is also a great place to visit, if you want to go to the beach, and the town itself is also quite charming. 
We drove to Miami during spring break, and stopped in Charleston and Savannah on the way, and especially Savannah really exceeded my expectations - both cities are absolutely beautiful, and rich with culture and history.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it surprisingly easy. Obviously, there will be some cultural differences, but I found it easy to kind of pick anc choose which aspects I wanted to adopt, and on which occasions I chose to hold on to more "european" values and customs ;)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: In my personal experience, living with local students really made a big difference. Similarly, making friends with exchanges students who also lived with local students, allowed me to create a substantial network of local friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It can at times, be challenging not to have a car. Biking is possible, but the infrastructure is just not really made for it, and people don't take care to look out for cyclists. I was lucky to have two roommates who had cars, so longer shopping trips for example were made easier when driving with them. It is possible to rent cars, but it isn't really that cheap - otherwise Uber is obviously an easy alternative. Also I think, especially living in Copenhagen, you have to get used to the fact that can't, or shouldn't, walk everywhere. This is both due to the long distances and infrstructre, but also as a safety precaution. I ended up buying a pepper spray (which is legal, and can be bought at Target) - not necessarily because I ever felt personally unsafe, but beacuse things did happen occasionally, and you might as well take the safety precautions available.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: There is definitely a different vibe at American colleges, because it is such an integral part of the students' life - as opposed to here, where most people have so many things going on outside of school. I really liked the feeling of belonging that that instilled in you as a student, whether it be hanging out on the quad during breaks, or at big sporting events. Specifically I really enjoyed the hospitality and friendliness, that I experienced in North Carolina and the surrounding states.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Don't be afraid to take time for yourself while you're away. You will probably experience an intense need to be social all the time (especially at the beginning), and that's perfectly fine and also important, but you're also gone for such a long time that you start establishing an everyday, and during that time it is perfectly fine - if not necessary - to take some time for yourself to read good books, talk to your friends/family at home or do something by yourself like a workout class or walking to Carrboro. 
Definitely take advantage of all the (free!) options for recreation - workout classes, clubs etc. 
You will definitely spend more than the estimated amount on your exchange in general, and also just while you're there. It's just more fun if you have financial wiggle room.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Even though it's a huge cliché, make sure you enjoy your time there and make the most of it! 
There's probably something else, but you'll figure it out in due time.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed making friends with the other exchange students, and generally just the feeling of making an everyday life for yourself in a new place and a foreign country. You have a different freedom, because there are a lot of obligations that you can leave behind at home, and that is quite unique.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I think there were two things that I found most challenging. First thing was being away from my boyfriend and my family. No matter how independent you might be, I don't think this is ever something you can work your way around. But you can of course make plans to talk/facetime and stuff like that, and that makes things a little easier. 
Second, I found the logistical aspects a little challenging. I had to open an American bank account in order to pay my rent, and that just proved incredibly challenging (partly because I hadn't gotten an American phone number at the time). In my experience, there were a lot of these practical/logistical things that I struggled with in the first month, but they all worked out, it just took a little time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I can almost guarantee, that you will not regret going on exchange - whether it be at UNC or anywhere else!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
